# 1.2 Habituation: getting used to what is always there {#sec-habituation}

<div data-life="status" data-stage="1.2h"></div>

The animals of the previous stage know good from bad, and they respond to a look in the same way every time they
see it. A bush that has just been emptied still has the colour of a full one, so the animal stands in front of it
and bites at nothing. What is missing is simple to say: an animal should stop responding to something that stays
the same and keeps giving nothing.

This stage changes one thing, in the eyes.

## The world: a bush that never has berries

The world of the previous stage gets one more kind of bush, a *dud*. It looks like a berry bush and never carries
a berry. Its colour is drawn anew for every life, so nothing an ancestor knew about colours can tell an animal to
leave it alone. In some lives the dud happens to have a colour the animal finds attractive, and then an animal
that responds to a look in the same way every time will stand at it and bite for as long as it lives.

There are as many bushes with berries as before; the duds come on top.

<div data-life="settings" data-stage="1.2h"></div>

::: {.callout-note title="What did not work: making the food unfamiliar"}
Without the dud, in the world of the previous stage, the change of this stage was used only a little. The long
lives had already selected most of the standing still away, and evolution can learn the look of an empty bush of
every kind it has always known.

Giving the good berries a new colour in every life did not change that. The animals with adapting eyes did
slightly worse than those without. What makes adaptation worth having is something that looks like food and
gives nothing, whatever colour it has.
:::

## The biology: adaptation and habituation

Step into a room with a strong smell and after a few minutes it is gone. The smell is still there; the receptors
have stopped reporting it. Sensory neurons respond to *change*: to what differs from the recent past. A steady
input is the background, and the background carries no news. This is *sensory adaptation*.

*Habituation* is the same thing seen in behaviour. A snail that is touched pulls in its horns. Touch it again and
again and it stops bothering. It is the simplest kind of learning there is, older than learning by association,
and found in every animal that has been tested, including ones with a few hundred neurons.

## The circuit

No new cells. Each of the eyes' **look** inputs now keeps a slow average of what it has been seeing, over
roughly the last fifty ticks, and passes on the difference between what it sees now and that average.

Two things follow, both for the whole brain, because every neuron downstream of the eyes now gets the adapted
look:

- **What stays in view fades.** An animal that stands in front of a bush sees its look sink into the average. The
  appetitive cells, driven by that look, fall silent, and with them the urge to bite. The animal moves on.
- **What is unusual stands out.** All berry bushes look alike in most respects, and that shared part is nearly
  always in view, so it is nearly always in the average. What passes through is the part that differs: the colour
  of this bush. Nothing uses this yet. It becomes important in the next stage, where the animal learns from a
  single bite which colour is bad.

<div data-life="brain" data-stage="1.2h"></div>

## Results

The control is the brain of the previous stage, with eyes that do not adapt, in the same world. Its fitness swings
from one generation to the next: every generation draws a new colour for the dud, and how well these animals do
depends on whether they happen to like it.

The first generations of main are a step back. Every synapse the animals inherit was shaped by eyes that reported
the whole look, and now reports only the difference. The population has to re-tune before the change can pay.

<div data-life="curves" data-stage="1.2h"></div>

<div data-life="summary" data-stage="1.2h"></div>

The test in which main and control animals share a world is left out for this stage. In that test both halves
run on the same brain, and here the difference *is* the brain's inputs: the control animals would be given
adapting eyes that none of their synapses were tuned to.

### Is it used?

There is no group of neurons to silence here, since the change is in how the inputs work. The matching test is to
switch the adaptation off in the final population and let the same animals live in the same worlds again.
